builder_plan.scenario: A support or data assistant repeats work across related customer requests.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's memory change in a replay of past tasks, with separate memory per customer.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current memory pipeline plus a no-memory control using the same agent.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Task success, stale memories, retrieval misses, response latency, and all memory maintenance costs.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: LeanSparse: Memory-Efficient Serving for Native Sparse-Attention LLMs
summary: LeanSparse replaces full on-GPU retention of indexer keys and monolithic prefill memory allocation in sparse-attention serving with layer-by-layer streamed prefill through reusable buffers and coarse-to-fine candidate retrieval over compact index representations. The cost is systems complexity: a modified SGLang runtime, separate indexer-key and KV caches, and dependency on models with native sparse attention (e.g., DeepSeek-V4-Flash), so the gains do not transfer to standard dense-attention models. It can fail if the coarse index pruning degrades retrieval quality for some workloads, if the implementation remains tied to a specific serving stack, or if the reader's actual context lengths are far below the regime where memory pressure justifies the added machinery.
rationale: The technique presupposes native sparse-attention foundation models and near-million-token contexts that a 24 GB GPU or API-based setup cannot host, so it is relevant only as a signal for future infrastructure decisions rather than an immediate adoption candidate.
technique: Layer-streamed prefill and coarse-to-fine sparse-attention serving

claims.statement: LeanSparse replaces full on-GPU retention of indexer keys and monolithic prefill memory allocation in sparse-attention serving with layer-by-layer streamed prefill through reusable buffers and coarse-to-fine candidate retrieval over compact index representations. The cost is systems complexity: a modified SGLang runtime, separate indexer-key and KV caches, and dependency on models with native sparse attention (e.g., DeepSeek-V4-Flash), so the gains do not transfer to standard dense-attention models. It can fail if the coarse index pruning degrades retrieval quality for some workloads, if the implementation remains tied to a specific serving stack, or if the reader's actual context lengths are far below the regime where memory pressure justifies the added machinery.

At 950K context on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, LeanSparse supports 2.95x as many concurrent requests and 2.14x decode throughput over HiSparse; on multi-turn Open-SWE traces it reduces median TTFT from 21.6s to 0.6s versus ECHO.
